newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU clears Lyonnaise des Eaux/Cie de Suez merger.
newsitem.headline: EU clears Lyonnaise des Eaux/Cie de Suez merger.

text.p: The European Commission on Thursday cleared the merger of French companies Lyonnaise des Eaux and Compagnie de Suez, creating a global utilities heavyweight.

It said after a one-month routine probe that the deal would not pose any competition problems in the markets concerned which range from energy, cable distribution and engineering to finance, mining and media.

The only concerns had arisen in the market for waste management in Belgium where the two partners would have held a "very strong position". But the parties agreed to sell part of their activities, it said in a statement.

The merger, which will have annual sales of more than 200 billion French francs ($34.3 billion) and a market capitalisation of 75 billion francs, was filed for EU regulatory approval at the end of April under EU rules which ban creation or strengthening of dominant positions.
The deal marks the end of the independence of Cie de Suez, set up in the 19th century to build the Suez canal, a triumph of French engineering.
The new group, to be called Suez/Lyonnaise, will focus on core businesses -- energy, water distribution, waste management and communications.
To assuage the Commission's concerns, Lyonnaise proposed selling the "major part" of its Belgian activities for the collection of domestic and industrial waste.
The two partners also agreed that one or the other would divest its interests in the field of detoxication of special industrial waste in Belgium.

"The divestment proposed practically removes the effects of the operation on the three markets where the position of the parties was very strong and allows for the emergence of a viable competitor," the statement said.

Waste management company Sita, a unit of Lyonnaise, said earlier this week that it would sell its minority stake in Page, which is controlled by Belgian steel company Cockerill Sambre, and other activities.
The Commission, the EU's competition watchdog, can set strict conditions for approving mergers and acquisitions found to harm fair competition in the 15-nation bloc. ($ = 5.825 French Francs)
